title: Space
blurb: Planets, stars, galaxies and the search for life.

lessons.title: The Solar System
lessons.summary: A tour of our neighbourhood, from the Sun to the edge.

cards.title: Our star
cards.text: The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in the Solar System. It's a ball of hot plasma, fusing hydrogen into helium in its core at about 15 million °C.

deep.x: The Sun is an ordinary star: a medium-sized yellow dwarf, one of perhaps 100–400 billion in the Milky Way. What makes it special is simply that it's ours. It is 1.39 million km wide, about 109 times Earth's diameter, and you could fit roughly 1.3 million Earths inside it.

In the core, the temperature is about 15 million °C and the pressure is about 250 billion times the air pressure at sea level. Under those conditions, hydrogen nuclei collide hard enough to fuse into helium. Every second the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium, and around 4 million tonnes of mass disappear as pure energy (E = mc²).
Why it doesn't explode or collapse

The Sun is a balancing act. Gravity squeezes inwards; the heat from fusion pushes outwards. If fusion speeds up, the core expands, cools slightly and fusion slows again. This self-regulation has kept the Sun stable for about 4.6 billion years.
What it's made of

x: About 73% hydrogen and 25% helium by mass
The remaining 2% is "metals" to astronomers: oxygen, carbon, iron and more
It rotates faster at its equator (about 25 days) than at its poles (about 35 days), because it isn't solid

deep.x: The light reaching you now left the Sun's surface about 8 minutes ago, but the energy behind it took tens of thousands of years to work its way out from the core.
The Sun loses about 4 million tonnes of mass every second, yet it's so big that over its whole life it will lose less than 0.1% of its mass this way.

cards.title: Eight planets
cards.text: Four small rocky planets sit close to the Sun; four giants lie further out. A memory trick: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming".

deep.x: The planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a flat, spinning disc of gas and dust around the young Sun. Close to the Sun it was too hot for ice, so only rock and metal could clump together: that's why the inner planets are small and rocky. Beyond the "snow line", between Mars and Jupiter, ice was plentiful, so cores grew big enough to grab huge amounts of gas.

steps: Spinning disc of gas and dust

deep.x: Why they all orbit the same way
All eight planets orbit in the same direction and roughly in the same plane, because they formed from the same spinning disc. It's a fossil of the Solar System's birth.

items: Most also spin the same way

deep.x: Quick profiles

x: **Mercury**: smallest, no real atmosphere, days scorching and nights freezing
**Venus**: Earth-sized, buried under thick clouds of sulphuric acid
**Earth**: the only place known to have life and liquid surface oceans
**Mars**: cold desert with the tallest volcano and a deep canyon system
**Jupiter**: largest, a gas giant with a storm bigger than Earth
**Saturn**: famous rings, lighter than water on average
**Uranus**: tilted on its side, an icy blue-green giant
**Neptune**: farthest, darkest and windiest

deep.w: The planets line up in a neat row
deep.r: They're spread around their orbits; true alignments are rare and loose

deep.x: The mnemonic "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming" gives the order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

cards.title: Rocky vs giant
cards.text: The inner planets are made of rock and metal. The outer ones are gas giants (Jupiter, Saturn) and ice giants (Uranus, Neptune), with no solid surface to stand on.

deep.x: The Solar System splits neatly in two. The four inner planets are dense balls of rock around iron cores. The four outer planets are giants: mostly gas and fluids, with no surface you could stand on.
Gas giants vs ice giants

Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium, like the Sun. Uranus and Neptune contain much more water, ammonia and methane, compressed into hot, dense fluids. Astronomers call those "ices" even though they aren't frozen.
What's inside Jupiter

Going down into Jupiter, the gas gets denser and hotter until hydrogen is squeezed into a liquid metal that conducts electricity. Swirling metallic hydrogen generates Jupiter's magnetic field, the strongest of any planet.
Why the split?

x: Near the Sun, only rock and metal could stay solid
Farther out, ice added extra building material, so cores grew faster
Big cores (about 10 Earth masses) could pull in surrounding gas before the young Sun blew it away

deep.x: Jupiter's magnetic field is about 20,000 times stronger than Earth's, and its radiation belts would be lethal to an unshielded astronaut.

cards.title: Venus is the hottest
cards.text: Venus is further from the Sun than Mercury but hotter, about 465 °C, because its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect.

deep.x: Venus shows what a runaway greenhouse effect can do. Its atmosphere is about 96% carbon dioxide and so thick that the surface pressure is 92 times Earth's, like being 900 metres under the sea.
How the trap works

Sunlight that gets through the clouds warms the ground. The ground gives off infrared heat, but CO₂ absorbs it and sends much of it back down. With so much CO₂, almost no heat escapes, and the whole planet sits at around 465 °C, day and night, poles and equator.

steps: Surface hot enough to melt lead

deep.x: Earth's twin gone wrong

Venus is almost Earth's size and was probably once much more like it, possibly with oceans. Being closer to the Sun, its water evaporated, strengthening the greenhouse effect until the oceans boiled away and the hydrogen leaked into space.
Other oddities

x: Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, so the Sun rises in the west
A day on Venus (243 Earth days) is longer than its year (225 Earth days)
Clouds of sulphuric acid race around the planet in about four days
Soviet Venera landers survived on the surface for only up to about two hours

deep.w: Mercury must be hottest because it's closest to the Sun
deep.r: Venus is hotter, thanks to its thick CO₂ atmosphere

deep.x: Distance from the Sun isn't everything: an atmosphere can matter more.

cards.title: Jupiter, the giant
cards.text: Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has lasted for centuries.

deep.x: Jupiter has 318 times Earth's mass, more than twice the mass of all the other planets combined. If it had been about 80 times more massive, it could have become a small star.
The Great Red Spot

The Great Red Spot is a giant anticyclone, a high-pressure storm, wider than Earth. It has been observed since at least the 1830s, maybe since 1665, but it's shrinking: it was about three Earths wide in the 1800s.
A fast spinner
Despite its size, Jupiter spins once in under 10 hours, the fastest of any planet. The spin flattens it visibly at the poles and stretches its clouds into the striped bands we see.
Moons and missions

x: About 95 known moons, including the four large Galilean moons Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto
Galileo discovered those four in 1610, proving not everything orbits Earth
NASA's Juno has orbited Jupiter since 2016, mapping its interior and poles
ESA's JUICE, launched 2023, will study the icy moons in the 2030s

deep.x: Jupiter doesn't strictly orbit the Sun's centre: the Sun and Jupiter both orbit a shared balance point just outside the Sun's surface.

cards.title: Saturn's rings
cards.text: Saturn's rings are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from dust to house-sized. They're about 280,000 km wide but in places only about 10 metres thick.

deep.x: Saturn's rings are mostly water ice, from tiny grains to chunks the size of a house. They stretch about 280,000 km across, almost three-quarters of the distance from Earth to the Moon, yet are often only about 10 metres thick. If the rings were a sheet of paper, they'd be far thinner than paper relative to their width.
How old are they?

Data from the Cassini spacecraft suggested the rings could be young, perhaps only a few hundred million years old, because they look clean and bright. Other scientists argue rings can stay clean for billions of years. It's still debated.
Where rings come from
Rings likely formed when a moon or comet came too close and was torn apart by Saturn's gravity. Inside a zone called the Roche limit, tidal forces stop material clumping into a moon.
Rings everywhere

x: All four giant planets have rings; Saturn's are simply the brightest
Gaps are cleared by small "shepherd moons" orbiting within the rings
The rings are slowly raining onto Saturn and may vanish in a few hundred million years

deep.x: Every 13–15 years Earth passes through the plane of Saturn's rings, and they almost disappear from view because they're so thin.

cards.title: Pluto, demoted
cards.text: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union defined a planet as a body that has cleared its orbit. Pluto shares its zone with many icy objects, so it became a dwarf planet.

deep.x: For 76 years Pluto was the ninth planet. Then astronomers began finding similar icy worlds beyond Neptune, in the Kuiper Belt. In 2005 they found Eris, about the same size as Pluto. Either it was a tenth planet, or the definition had to change.
The three rules
In 2006 the International Astronomical Union said a planet must meet three criteria. Pluto passes the first two but fails the third.

items: Round, shaped by its own gravity

deep.x: What New Horizons found

In 2015 NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto and revealed a surprisingly active world: a heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice, mountains of water ice, a thin hazy atmosphere and signs of a possible underground ocean.
Still controversial

x: Some planetary scientists prefer a geology-based definition: any round world is a planet
Under that rule, the Solar System would have dozens of planets
Officially, there are five recognised dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake

deep.w: Pluto was demoted because it's too small
deep.r: It hasn't cleared its orbit of other objects

deep.x: Science reclassifies things when new evidence shows the old categories no longer fit.

cards.title: Asteroids and comets
cards.text: Asteroids are rocky leftovers, mostly between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies from the outer Solar System that grow glowing tails when they near the Sun.

deep.x: Asteroids and comets are leftovers from the formation of the planets, 4.6 billion years old. Studying them is like reading the Solar System's original building materials.
Asteroid types

x: **C-type**: dark, carbon-rich, the most common
**S-type**: stony, made of silicate minerals
**M-type**: metallic, possibly cores of shattered protoplanets

deep.x: A comet's journey

Most of the time a comet is a dark, frozen lump far from the Sun. As it approaches, sunlight turns ice directly into gas, which drags dust out with it. That creates a glowing coma and two tails: a straight blue ion tail pushed by the solar wind, and a curved, yellowish dust tail.
Samples brought home

Missions have collected pieces of asteroids and returned them to Earth: Japan's Hayabusa2 from Ryugu (2020) and NASA's OSIRIS-REx from Bennu (2023). Bennu's sample contained water-bearing minerals and organic molecules, ingredients for life.
Comets and water-rich asteroids may have delivered some of Earth's water and organic molecules early in its history.

cards.title: Distances
cards.text: Astronomers measure the Solar System in astronomical units: 1 AU is the Earth–Sun distance, about 150 million km. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us.

deep.x: Space distances are so large that kilometres become clumsy. Astronomers use the astronomical unit (AU), the average Earth–Sun distance of about 149.6 million km, for the Solar System, and light-years for the stars.
Light travel times

x: Moon: 1.3 seconds
Sun: 8 minutes 20 seconds
Jupiter: 35–52 minutes, depending on positions
Neptune: about 4 hours
Voyager 1: over 23 hours

v.unit: light travel time from the Sun, minutes

deep.x: How we measure it

Astronomers bounce radar off Venus and asteroids and time the echo, giving the AU to within metres. For nearby stars, they use parallax: the tiny shift in a star's position as Earth moves around the Sun.
Communicating with distant spacecraft is slow: commands to a Mars rover can take up to 24 minutes to arrive, so rovers must drive partly by themselves.
Travelling at motorway speed, 120 km/h, it would take about 140 years to drive to the Sun.

cards.title: A model in a football stadium
cards.text: Shrink the Sun to a football in the centre circle. Earth is a peppercorn about 25 m away, Jupiter a marble about 130 m away, and Neptune a small bead about 715 m away.

deep.x: Scale models reveal just how empty the Solar System is. Shrink the Sun to a football 22 cm wide, about 6.3 billion times smaller than reality, and every distance shrinks by the same factor.

x: Scale = 1 : 6.3 billion
Earth–Sun 150 million km → 24 m
Earth 12,742 km → 2 mm

deep.x: Where everything goes

x: **Mercury**: a grain of sand, 9 m away
**Venus** and **Earth**: two peppercorns, 17 m and 24 m away
**Mars**: a pinhead, 36 m away
**Jupiter**: a marble, 124 m away
**Saturn**: a smaller marble, 227 m away
**Uranus** and **Neptune**: two peas or beads, 455 m and 715 m away

deep.x: And the nearest star?
On the same scale, Proxima Centauri would be another football about 6,400 km away, farther than from Lisbon to New York.

deep.w: Space is crowded like in films
deep.r: The Solar System is almost entirely empty space

deep.x: Try it: pace out the distances in a park with a ball and some peppercorns. It's the best way to feel the scale.

quiz.q: Which planet is the hottest?
quiz.explain: Its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat.

quiz.q: How long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
quiz.explain: The Sun is 150 million km away.

quiz.q: Why was Pluto reclassified in 2006?

lessons.title: Stars and galaxies
lessons.summary: How stars live and die, and where we are in the universe.

cards.title: A star is born
cards.text: Stars form inside giant clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls a clump together until the core is hot and dense enough to fuse hydrogen, and a star lights up.

cards.title: Fusion
cards.text: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. A little mass is turned into a lot of energy, following Einstein's E = mc².

cards.title: Star colours
cards.text: A star's colour shows its temperature: red stars are the coolest, blue the hottest. Our Sun is a yellowish-white star in the middle.

cards.title: Life of a star like the Sun
cards.text: The Sun is about halfway through a 10-billion-year life. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a red giant, then shed its outer layers and leave a small white dwarf.

cards.title: Death of a giant star
cards.text: Stars much heavier than the Sun end in a supernova explosion that can briefly outshine a galaxy. The core becomes a neutron star or, if heavy enough, a black hole.

cards.title: We are stardust
cards.text: Most of the atoms in your body, like carbon, oxygen and iron, were made inside stars that exploded before the Sun was born.

cards.title: Black holes
cards.text: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope took the first image of one, in the galaxy M87.

cards.title: Light-years
cards.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 9.5 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.title: The Milky Way
cards.text: Our galaxy is a barred spiral of 100–400 billion stars, about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits in a quiet arm about 26,000 light-years from the centre.

cards.title: Billions of galaxies
cards.text: The observable universe holds perhaps 100 billion to 2 trillion galaxies. The Andromeda galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away, is the furthest thing you can see with the naked eye.

quiz.q: What powers stars?
Which colour stars are the hottest?
What will the Sun become at the end of its life?
quiz.explain: It's not massive enough to explode.

lessons.title: Space exploration
lessons.summary: From Sputnik to Mars rovers.

cards.title: The Space Race
cards.text: After the Second World War, the USA and the Soviet Union competed to reach space first. The Soviets launched the first satellite and the first human; the Americans landed on the Moon.

cards.title: How rockets work

steps: Hot gas rushes out the back

cards.text: Rockets push hot gas out of the back at high speed; by Newton's third law, the gas pushes the rocket forward. They work in a vacuum because they carry their own oxygen.

cards.title: Getting to orbit
cards.text: To orbit, you need to go sideways fast enough to keep "falling" around the Earth without hitting it: about 7.8 km/s, or 28,000 km/h, in low orbit.

cards.title: Apollo 11
cards.text: On 20 July 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above. Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972.

cards.title: The International Space Station
cards.text: The ISS has been continuously crewed since November 2000. It's about the size of a football pitch and circles the Earth about 16 times a day.

cards.title: Space telescopes
cards.text: Above the atmosphere, telescopes see more clearly. Hubble (1990) transformed astronomy; James Webb (2021) sees infrared light from the first galaxies.

cards.title: Robots on Mars
cards.text: Rovers have explored Mars since 1997. Perseverance, landed in 2021, collects rock samples and carried Ingenuity, the first helicopter to fly on another planet.

cards.title: Reusable rockets
cards.text: Since 2015, rockets have landed their boosters back on Earth to fly again. Reuse has cut the cost of reaching orbit and made launches routine.

cards.title: Voyager
cards.text: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object, more than 24 billion km away. It carries a golden record of sounds and images from Earth.

cards.title: Satellites in daily life
cards.text: Thousands of satellites support daily life: GPS navigation, weather forecasts, TV, internet and monitoring of fires and crops.

quiz.q: Who was the first human in space?
Why can rockets work in space without air?

lessons.title: Earth, Moon and sky
lessons.summary: Seasons, phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.title: Why we have seasons

items.w: Closer to the Sun in summer
items.r: Earth's tilt changes the angle of sunlight

cards.text: Seasons aren't caused by distance from the Sun. Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°, so each hemisphere takes turns leaning towards the Sun and getting more direct light.

cards.title: Day and night
cards.text: Earth spins on its axis once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the other side has night. The Sun "rises" because we turn towards it.

cards.title: Moon phases
cards.text: The Moon doesn't make light; it reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth every 29.5 days, we see different amounts of its lit half.

cards.title: The far side

items.r: the far side, which gets sunlight too

cards.text: The Moon always shows us the same face because it spins exactly once per orbit, known as tidal locking. The far side isn't dark; it gets as much sunlight as the near side.

cards.title: Solar eclipses
cards.text: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth. By coincidence, the Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times further away, so they look the same size.

cards.title: Lunar eclipses
cards.text: In a lunar eclipse, Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. The Moon turns coppery red because Earth's atmosphere bends red sunlight onto it.

cards.title: Tides
cards.text: The Moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, creating two bulges of water: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side. As Earth turns, most coasts get two high tides a day.

cards.title: Where the Moon came from
cards.text: The leading theory: about 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body called Theia crashed into the young Earth, and the debris came together to form the Moon.

cards.title: Shooting stars
cards.text: Meteors are specks of dust burning up in the atmosphere at tens of km per second. Meteor showers like the Perseids (August) happen when Earth crosses a comet's trail.

cards.title: Spotting planets

items: Jupiter: bright all night when visible

cards.text: Planets don't twinkle as much as stars and move slowly against the background over weeks. Venus is often the brightest "star" right after sunset or before dawn.

quiz.q: What causes the seasons?
quiz.explain: The tilt changes the angle of sunlight.

quiz.q: Why does the Moon look red in a lunar eclipse?
options: Earth's atmosphere bends red light onto it
quiz.explain: Like all the sunsets on Earth at once.

lessons.title: Life in the universe
lessons.summary: Exoplanets, aliens and the big questions.

cards.title: Exoplanets
cards.text: An exoplanet orbits a star other than the Sun. The first around a Sun-like star was found in 1995; today more than 5,000 are confirmed.

cards.title: Finding them

steps: A planet is passing in front

cards.text: Most exoplanets are found by the transit method: when a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims slightly and regularly.

cards.title: The Goldilocks zone
cards.text: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where it's neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water on a planet's surface.

cards.title: What life needs
cards.text: Life as we know it needs liquid water, an energy source and chemistry built around carbon. On Earth, microbes live in boiling springs, ice and deep rock.

cards.title: Places to look nearby
cards.text: Mars may once have had rivers; Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus have oceans under their ice, and Enceladus sprays water into space.

cards.title: The Drake equation

viz.f: N = R* · fp · ne · fl · fi · fc · L

cards.text: In 1961 Frank Drake listed the factors needed to estimate how many civilisations might be signalling in our galaxy. Most of the numbers are still unknown.

cards.title: The Fermi paradox
cards.text: If the galaxy is old and huge, why haven't we met anyone? Possible answers: life is rare, civilisations don't last, distances are too vast, or we're not looking the right way.

cards.title: SETI
cards.text: The Search for Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence listens for radio signals from other civilisations. The famous 1977 "Wow! signal" was never detected again.

cards.title: Messages we sent
cards.text: In 1974 the Arecibo radio telescope beamed a message towards a star cluster 25,000 light-years away. The Voyager golden records carry greetings in 55 languages.

cards.title: The pale blue dot
cards.text: In 1990, Voyager 1 photographed Earth from about 6 billion km away: a speck of light less than a pixel wide. Carl Sagan used it to remind us how small and precious our world is.

quiz.q: How are most exoplanets found?
options: A star dims as a planet passes

quiz.q: Which moon sprays water from a hidden ocean?

lessons.title: Mars, the red planet
lessons.summary: Our most explored neighbour.

cards.title: Why it's red
cards.text: Mars is red because its dust is rich in iron oxide: rust. The fine dust gets everywhere, even tinting the sky a butterscotch colour.

cards.title: A small, cold world
cards.text: Mars is about half Earth's width with roughly a third of its gravity. The average temperature is around −65 °C, and the air is 100 times thinner than ours.

cards.title: Day and year
cards.text: A Martian day, called a sol, lasts 24 h 37 min, very close to ours. A Martian year is 687 Earth days, so its seasons last about twice as long.

cards.title: Olympus Mons
cards.text: Mars has the tallest volcano in the Solar System: Olympus Mons, about 22 km high, two and a half times the height of Everest, and about 600 km wide, roughly the length of Portugal.

cards.title: Valles Marineris
cards.text: A canyon system about 4,000 km long and up to 7 km deep cuts across Mars. On Earth it would stretch roughly from Lisbon to Moscow.

cards.title: Water on Mars
cards.text: Dry riverbeds, deltas and minerals that form in water show Mars once had lakes and rivers. Today water survives as ice at the poles and underground.

cards.title: Two tiny moons
cards.text: Mars has two small, lumpy moons, Phobos and Deimos, probably captured asteroids or debris from an impact. Phobos is slowly spiralling inwards.

cards.title: Dust storms
cards.text: Mars has dust storms that can cover the whole planet for weeks. A 2018 storm ended the Opportunity rover's mission by blocking sunlight to its solar panels.

cards.title: Getting there
cards.text: Launch windows to Mars open about every 26 months, when the planets line up. The trip takes six to nine months.

cards.title: Living on Mars?
cards.text: Humans on Mars would need shelter from radiation and cold, oxygen made from CO₂, and water dug from ice. It's possible, but far harder than living in Antarctica.

quiz.q: Why is Mars red?
How long is a Martian day?
What is Olympus Mons?
options: The tallest volcano in the Solar System

lessons.title: Giant planets and their moons
lessons.summary: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and their worlds.

cards.title: Gas and ice giants
cards.text: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune have more water, ammonia and methane "ices", which is why they're called ice giants.

cards.title: Jupiter's protection?
cards.text: Jupiter's huge gravity flings or captures many comets and asteroids. It may shield the inner planets, though it can also send some our way.

cards.title: Io, the volcanic moon
cards.text: Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanic place known, with hundreds of volcanoes. Jupiter's gravity squeezes it like a stress ball, heating its interior.

cards.title: Europa's ocean
cards.text: Under Europa's icy crust lies a salty ocean with perhaps twice the water of all Earth's oceans. NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will study it.

cards.title: Ganymede
cards.text: Ganymede, another moon of Jupiter, is the largest moon in the Solar System, bigger than the planet Mercury, and has its own magnetic field.

cards.title: Titan
cards.text: Saturn's moon Titan has a thick orange atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane and ethane. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005.

cards.title: Saturn floats
cards.text: Saturn's average density is lower than water's. Given a big enough bathtub, it would float, although it's a ball of gas, not a solid.

cards.title: Uranus on its side
cards.text: Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it rolls around the Sun on its side. Each pole gets 42 years of continuous daylight and then 42 years of night.

cards.title: Neptune's winds
cards.text: Neptune, the farthest planet, has the fastest winds in the Solar System, above 2,000 km/h. It was found in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it.

cards.title: Visits to the giants
cards.text: Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus and Neptune, in 1986 and 1989. Galileo and Juno studied Jupiter; Cassini orbited Saturn for 13 years.

quiz.q: Which moon is the largest in the Solar System?
Why is Io so volcanic?
How was Neptune discovered?

lessons.title: The Sun up close
lessons.summary: Our star and its moods.

cards.title: Layers of the Sun
cards.text: Energy is made in the core, then crawls outwards through the radiative zone over tens of thousands of years, bubbles up through the convective zone and escapes from the surface.

cards.title: Hot and hotter
cards.text: The surface is about 5,500 °C, but the outer atmosphere, the corona, reaches over a million degrees. Why it's so hot is still being studied.

cards.title: Sunspots
cards.text: Sunspots are cooler, darker patches where magnetic fields block heat. Their numbers rise and fall over an 11-year solar cycle.

cards.title: Solar flares
cards.text: Flares are sudden bursts of energy from tangled magnetic fields. Big ones can disrupt radio, GPS and satellites on Earth.

cards.title: Solar wind
cards.text: The Sun constantly blows charged particles into space at around 400 km/s. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of them.

cards.title: Auroras
cards.text: When solar particles hit the upper atmosphere near the poles, oxygen glows green and red, and nitrogen glows blue and purple: the northern and southern lights.

cards.title: The Carrington Event
cards.text: In 1859 a huge solar storm made auroras visible near the tropics and gave telegraph operators electric shocks. A similar storm today could damage power grids.

cards.title: Space weather forecasts
cards.text: Spacecraft watch the Sun to warn of storms a day or more ahead, so satellite and grid operators can prepare.

cards.title: Never look directly
cards.text: Looking at the Sun, even briefly during a partial eclipse, can permanently damage your retina. Use certified eclipse glasses or project the image.

cards.title: Parker Solar Probe
cards.text: Launched in 2018, NASA's Parker Solar Probe has flown through the corona and is the fastest human-made object, reaching about 690,000 km/h.

quiz.q: What causes sunspots?
What makes auroras?
options: Solar particles hitting the upper atmosphere

lessons.title: The Big Bang
lessons.summary: How the universe began and grew.

cards.title: An expanding universe
cards.text: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are, the faster. Space itself is expanding.

cards.title: Run it backwards
cards.text: If everything is moving apart, it was once closer together. Run the film back about 13.8 billion years and everything was extremely hot and dense: the Big Bang.

cards.title: Not an explosion in space
cards.text: The Big Bang wasn't a bomb going off in empty space. It was the rapid expansion of space itself, everywhere at once.

cards.title: Raisin bread
cards.text: Imagine raisins in rising dough: every raisin sees all the others moving away, and the farthest move fastest. There's no centre.

cards.title: The first minutes
cards.text: Within the first three minutes, the universe cooled enough for protons and neutrons to form hydrogen and helium nuclei. Heavier elements came much later, from stars.

cards.title: The afterglow
cards.text: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe became transparent. That light still fills space as faint microwaves, found by accident in 1965.

cards.title: Redshift
cards.text: Light from receding galaxies is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths, like a siren dropping in pitch as it drives away.

cards.title: The observable universe
cards.text: We can only see as far as light has had time to reach us. Because space expanded meanwhile, the edge of what we see is about 46 billion light-years away.

cards.title: Who named it?
cards.text: Fred Hoyle, who preferred a "steady state" universe, coined "Big Bang" on BBC radio in 1949. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian priest and physicist, first proposed the idea.

cards.title: How will it end?
cards.text: Most evidence points to a universe expanding forever, getting colder and darker over unimaginable time: the "heat death". Other endings are still debated.

quiz.q: How old is the universe?
quiz.explain: Measured from the expansion and afterglow.

quiz.q: What did Hubble discover in 1929?
options: Galaxies are moving away from us

lessons.title: Black holes
lessons.summary: The strangest objects in the universe.

cards.title: The event horizon

items: Event horizon: point of no return

cards.text: A black hole's boundary is the event horizon: the point of no return. Inside, the escape speed exceeds the speed of light.

cards.title: How they form
cards.text: Most stellar black holes form when a star more than about 20 times the Sun's mass runs out of fuel and its core collapses.

cards.title: Size
cards.text: If the Sun became a black hole, its event horizon would be only about 6 km across. Earth's would be the size of a marble.

cards.title: Supermassive black holes
cards.text: Almost every big galaxy has a supermassive black hole at its centre. Ours, Sagittarius A*, is about 4 million times the Sun's mass.

cards.title: Spaghettification
cards.text: Near a small black hole, gravity pulls far harder on your feet than your head, stretching you like spaghetti.

cards.title: Time slows down
cards.text: Near a black hole, time runs slower compared with far away. To a distant observer, something falling in seems to freeze at the edge.

cards.title: Seeing the invisible
cards.text: Black holes are found by their effects: stars orbiting something invisible, glowing hot gas swirling around them and ripples in spacetime.

cards.title: Gravitational waves
cards.text: In 2015 the LIGO detectors caught ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away, as Einstein had predicted a century earlier.

cards.title: The first image
cards.text: In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope, linking radio dishes across the world into an Earth-sized telescope, imaged the shadow of M87's black hole. Sagittarius A* followed in 2022.

cards.title: Hawking radiation
cards.text: Stephen Hawking calculated in 1974 that black holes should slowly leak energy and eventually evaporate, though for real ones this takes far longer than the universe's age.

quiz.q: What is the event horizon?
quiz.explain: Not even light escapes from inside.

quiz.q: What did LIGO detect in 2015?

lessons.title: Telescopes and light
lessons.summary: How we see the invisible universe.

cards.title: Looking back in time
cards.text: Light takes time to travel, so we see the Moon as it was 1.3 seconds ago, the Sun 8 minutes ago and Andromeda 2.5 million years ago.

cards.title: Galileo's telescope
cards.text: In 1609–10 Galileo pointed a simple telescope at the sky and saw Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots and countless stars in the Milky Way.

cards.title: Refractors and reflectors
cards.text: Refracting telescopes use lenses; reflecting telescopes, invented by Newton, use curved mirrors. All big research telescopes are reflectors, because mirrors can be made huge.

cards.title: Bigger is better
cards.text: A telescope's power to collect light depends on its mirror area. The upcoming Extremely Large Telescope in Chile has a 39 m mirror.

cards.title: The electromagnetic spectrum
cards.text: Visible light is a tiny slice of the spectrum. Different wavelengths reveal different things, from cold dust in radio to exploding stars in X-rays.

cards.title: Infrared
cards.text: Infrared light passes through dust clouds and shows cool objects. James Webb sees in infrared to spot newborn stars and the first galaxies, whose light was stretched by expansion.

cards.title: Why go to space?
cards.text: Earth's atmosphere blurs starlight and blocks X-rays, UV and much infrared. Space telescopes avoid both problems.

cards.title: Radio telescopes
cards.text: Radio telescopes are giant dishes. Linking dishes across continents creates a virtual telescope as wide as the distance between them.

cards.title: Spectroscopy
cards.text: Splitting starlight into a rainbow reveals dark lines: fingerprints of the elements in the star. That's how we know what stars are made of without visiting.

cards.title: Dark skies
cards.text: Light pollution hides most stars from city dwellers. Portugal's Dark Sky Alqueva reserve was the world's first "Starlight Tourism Destination", certified in 2011.

quiz.q: Why do we see Andromeda as it was 2.5 million years ago?
options: Its light took that long to reach us
quiz.explain: Light travels at a finite speed.

quiz.q: How do we know what stars are made of?
Why does Webb see in infrared?
options: Light from early galaxies is stretched to infrared

lessons.title: Gravity and orbits
lessons.summary: Why things fall, and why the Moon doesn't.

cards.title: Newton's gravity
cards.text: Isaac Newton realised the force that makes an apple fall also keeps the Moon in orbit. Every mass attracts every other mass.

cards.title: The inverse square law
cards.text: Double the distance and gravity drops to a quarter. Triple it and it drops to a ninth.

cards.title: Orbits are falling

steps: Fast enough: falls around the Earth

cards.text: An orbiting spacecraft is constantly falling towards Earth but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it. Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain.

cards.title: Weightlessness

items.r: Gravity is ~90% as strong, they're in free fall

cards.text: Astronauts on the ISS feel weightless not because there's no gravity, which is about 90% as strong there, but because they're falling together with the station.

cards.title: Mass and weight
cards.text: Your mass stays the same everywhere; your weight depends on gravity. A 70 kg person would weigh about as much as 12 kg on the Moon.

cards.title: Kepler's laws
cards.text: Johannes Kepler found that planets move in ellipses, sweep equal areas in equal times and that farther planets take longer to orbit.

cards.title: Escape velocity
cards.text: To escape Earth's gravity completely, you'd need about 11.2 km/s. On the Moon, just 2.4 km/s.

cards.title: Gravity assists
cards.text: Spacecraft swing past planets to steal a bit of their orbital speed, like a ball bouncing off a moving train. Voyager used Jupiter and Saturn this way.

cards.title: Lagrange points

items.b: between Sun and Earth, solar observatories

cards.text: There are five points where a small object can hold position relative to two big bodies. Webb sits at L2, 1.5 million km from Earth, opposite the Sun.

cards.title: Geostationary orbit
cards.text: At about 36,000 km up, a satellite orbits once a day, staying over the same spot. TV satellite dishes point at a fixed point in the sky for this reason.

quiz.q: Why are astronauts on the ISS weightless?
options: They're in free fall with the station
quiz.explain: Gravity is still about 90% as strong.

quiz.q: Double the distance, and gravity becomes…

lessons.title: Time, space and Einstein
lessons.summary: Relativity without the maths homework.

cards.title: The speed of light

items.l: laps of Earth in a second

cards.text: Light travels at about 300,000 km per second in a vacuum, and every observer measures the same speed, however fast they move. That simple fact changes everything.

cards.title: Time dilation
cards.text: Moving clocks run slow. An astronaut travelling near light speed would return to find more time had passed on Earth than for them.

cards.title: The twin paradox
cards.text: One twin flies to a star at 87% of light speed and back; the other stays home. On return, the traveller has aged about half as much. Time dilation itself has been confirmed with atomic clocks flown on planes.

cards.title: Length contraction
cards.text: Objects moving very fast are shorter in their direction of motion, as measured by someone watching them pass. It's only noticeable near light speed.

cards.title: E = mc²

items.m: speed of light squared, a huge number

cards.text: Mass and energy are two forms of the same thing. A tiny amount of mass holds huge energy, which powers the Sun and nuclear reactors.

cards.title: Gravity bends spacetime
cards.text: In general relativity (1915), mass curves spacetime and objects follow the curves. Think of a heavy ball on a trampoline making marbles roll towards it.

cards.title: Light bends
cards.text: In 1919, Arthur Eddington measured starlight bending around the Sun during an eclipse, exactly as Einstein predicted. It made Einstein world famous.

cards.title: GPS needs relativity
cards.text: GPS satellites' clocks run faster by about 38 microseconds a day because of weaker gravity and slower because of speed. Without corrections, positions would drift by kilometres daily.

cards.title: Gravitational lensing
cards.text: Massive galaxy clusters bend light from galaxies behind them, creating arcs and multiple images. Astronomers use these natural magnifying glasses.

cards.title: Nothing faster than light
cards.text: Nothing with mass can reach light speed: the closer you get, the more energy each extra bit of speed costs. Information can't travel faster than light either.

quiz.q: What happens to a clock moving very fast?
Why does GPS need relativity?
options: Satellite clocks run at a different rate
quiz.explain: Uncorrected, errors grow by km a day.

lessons.title: Life as an astronaut
lessons.summary: Eating, sleeping and working in orbit.

cards.title: Becoming an astronaut
cards.text: Space agencies pick a handful from thousands of applicants. ESA's 2022 selection drew over 22,500 applications for 17 places, including astronauts and reserves.

cards.title: Training
cards.text: Astronauts train for years: spacewalks rehearsed underwater, survival training, Russian language, robotics and flights in planes that create short bursts of weightlessness.

cards.title: Eating in space
cards.text: Food comes in pouches and tins; crumbs are dangerous, so tortillas replace bread. Taste dulls in orbit, so astronauts love spicy sauces.

cards.title: Sleeping

items: Sleeping bag tied to the wall

cards.text: Astronauts sleep in small cabins in sleeping bags tied to the wall. There's no "up", so you can sleep in any orientation.

cards.title: Bodies in space
cards.text: Without gravity, muscles and bones weaken, fluids shift to the head, and the spine stretches; astronauts grow about 3 cm taller temporarily.

cards.title: Exercise

items.l: bone lost a month without it

cards.text: To fight bone and muscle loss, ISS crews exercise about two hours a day on a treadmill with harnesses, a bike and a resistance machine.

cards.title: Water recycling
cards.text: On the ISS, about 98% of water, including sweat and urine, is recycled into clean drinking water.

cards.title: Spacewalks
cards.text: Spacewalks last six to eight hours. The suit is a mini spaceship with oxygen, cooling and pressure. Astronauts stay tethered at all times.

cards.title: The overview effect
cards.text: Many astronauts describe a shift in perspective after seeing Earth from space: a fragile blue ball with no visible borders.

cards.title: Coming home
cards.text: After months in orbit, astronauts need weeks to readapt: balance is shaky, and things feel heavy. Some forget gravity and let go of objects mid-air.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts eat tortillas instead of bread?
Why do astronauts get taller in space?

lessons.title: Stargazing
lessons.summary: Finding your way around the night sky.

cards.title: Constellations

items.l: stars visible on a dark night

cards.text: Constellations are patterns of stars named by ancient cultures. Astronomers recognise 88 official ones. Their stars are usually not close to each other in space.

cards.title: Finding the North Star
cards.text: Follow the two end stars of the Big Dipper's "bowl" upwards about five times their distance to reach Polaris, which barely moves and marks north.

cards.title: The sky turns
cards.text: Stars rise in the east and set in the west because Earth rotates. Long-exposure photos turn stars into circles around the celestial pole.

cards.title: Seasonal stars
cards.text: As Earth orbits the Sun, we see different constellations at night through the year. Orion rules winter evenings; Scorpius summer ones.

cards.title: Orion
cards.text: Orion is easy to find: three bright stars in a row form his belt. Red Betelgeuse marks a shoulder and blue Rigel a foot.

cards.title: Star brightness
cards.text: Astronomers measure brightness in magnitudes: lower numbers are brighter. Sirius, the brightest night star, is −1.5; the faintest naked-eye stars are about +6.

cards.title: Planets wander

steps: A month later: moved against the stars

cards.text: "Planet" comes from the Greek for "wanderer": planets move against the background stars over weeks, staying close to the Sun's path, the ecliptic.

cards.title: The Milky Way band
cards.text: On a dark night, a pale band arches across the sky: the combined light of billions of stars in our galaxy's disc, seen edge-on from inside.

cards.title: Using your eyes

items: Look slightly to the side of faint objects

cards.text: Your eyes need 20–30 minutes in darkness to fully adapt. Use a red light to read maps, because red barely disturbs night vision.

cards.title: A first night out
cards.text: Pick a moonless night, go away from lights, start with the Moon or a bright planet, then find Orion or the Big Dipper. Binoculars show far more than you'd expect.

quiz.q: How do you find Polaris?
options: Use the Big Dipper's pointer stars

quiz.q: Which is brighter: magnitude 1 or magnitude 5?

lessons.title: Asteroids, comets and impacts
lessons.summary: Space rocks and how we defend Earth.

cards.title: The asteroid belt

items.w: A crowded field of tumbling rocks
items.r: Mostly empty space, probes fly through safely

cards.text: Between Mars and Jupiter orbit millions of rocky bodies. Despite films, they're spread out: spacecraft cross the belt without dodging anything.

cards.title: Ceres
cards.text: Ceres, the largest object in the asteroid belt at about 940 km wide, is classed as a dwarf planet. NASA's Dawn found bright salt deposits on its surface.

cards.title: Comet anatomy

items: Tails: point away from the Sun
Nucleus: icy core, a few km

cards.text: A comet is a "dirty snowball" of ice and dust a few km wide. Near the Sun, ice turns to gas, forming a glowing head and tails that always point away from the Sun.

cards.title: Halley's Comet
cards.text: Edmond Halley predicted in 1705 that a comet seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 would return in 1758. It did, after his death. It next returns in 2061.

cards.title: Where comets come from
cards.text: Short-period comets come from the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune; long-period ones from the distant Oort Cloud, a shell perhaps a light-year away.

cards.title: The dinosaur killer
cards.text: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid around 10 km wide hit Mexico's Yucatán, making the Chicxulub crater. Dust and fires changed the climate and ended the non-bird dinosaurs.

cards.title: Tunguska
cards.text: In 1908 an object exploded over Siberia, flattening about 80 million trees over 2,000 km². Nobody was killed because the area was so remote.

cards.title: Chelyabinsk
cards.text: In 2013 a 20-metre rock exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia. The shock wave shattered windows and injured about 1,500 people, mostly from flying glass.

cards.title: Planetary defence
cards.text: Telescopes track near-Earth asteroids. In 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the moonlet Dimorphos and changed its orbit: the first test of deflecting an asteroid.

cards.title: How worried should we be?
cards.text: Small rocks hit every day and burn up. Bigger impacts are rare: city-destroying ones about every few centuries, and dinosaur-killers every ~100 million years.

quiz.q: Which way do a comet's tails point?
quiz.explain: Pushed by sunlight and solar wind.

quiz.q: What did NASA's DART mission show?
options: A spacecraft can change an asteroid's orbit

quiz.q: Where is Ceres?

lessons.title: Dark matter and dark energy
lessons.summary: The 95% of the universe we can't see.

cards.title: What the universe is made of
cards.text: Ordinary matter, everything made of atoms, is only about 5% of the universe. The rest is dark matter and dark energy, which we can't see directly.

cards.title: Spinning too fast
cards.text: In the 1970s Vera Rubin found that stars at galaxy edges orbit as fast as those near the centre. Visible matter alone couldn't hold them; something unseen adds gravity.

cards.title: Fritz Zwicky
cards.text: Back in 1933, Fritz Zwicky noticed galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by visible matter. He called the missing mass "dunkle Materie", dark matter.

cards.title: The Bullet Cluster
cards.text: When two galaxy clusters collided, the hot gas slowed down, but most of the mass, mapped by lensing, passed straight through: strong evidence for dark matter.

cards.title: What could it be?
cards.text: Dark matter doesn't emit or absorb light and barely interacts. Candidates include unknown particles like WIMPs or axions. Detectors deep underground have found nothing so far.

cards.title: Dark energy
cards.text: In 1998 two teams found that the universe's expansion is speeding up, not slowing. Something, called dark energy, pushes space apart. It won the 2011 Nobel Prize.

cards.title: Standard candles
cards.text: Type Ia supernovae all peak at about the same brightness, so how bright they look tells us how far away they are, like judging distance by a known light bulb.

cards.title: The cosmic web
cards.text: On the largest scales, galaxies form a web of filaments and walls around huge empty voids, shaped by dark matter's gravity.

cards.title: Euclid
cards.text: ESA's Euclid telescope, launched in 2023, is mapping billions of galaxies to measure how dark matter and dark energy shaped the universe.

cards.title: Science at the edge
cards.text: Dark matter and dark energy are names for things we can measure but don't yet understand. Not knowing is where the most exciting science happens.

quiz.q: What fraction of the universe is ordinary matter?
quiz.explain: The rest is dark matter and dark energy.

quiz.q: What is dark energy linked to?
options: The accelerating expansion of the universe

lessons.title: Satellites and GPS
lessons.summary: The invisible machines above us.

cards.title: How many?
cards.text: Over 10,000 active satellites orbit Earth, most launched in the last few years for internet constellations. The first, Sputnik, launched in 1957.

cards.title: Orbit types
cards.text: Satellites sit in different orbits for different jobs: low orbit for imaging and internet, medium for navigation, geostationary for TV and weather.

cards.title: How GPS works
cards.text: Your phone receives time signals from at least four satellites. From the tiny differences in arrival time, it calculates its position to within a few metres.

cards.title: Why four satellites?
cards.text: Three satellites fix your position in 3D; a fourth corrects your phone's cheap, imprecise clock. More satellites improve accuracy.

cards.title: Galileo
cards.text: Europe's own navigation system, Galileo, has over 25 satellites. Phones combine GPS (USA), Galileo (EU), GLONASS (Russia) and BeiDou (China).

cards.title: Weather satellites
cards.text: Geostationary satellites photograph the same half of Earth every few minutes, while polar orbiters scan the whole planet twice a day. Forecasts depend on both.

cards.title: Earth observation
cards.text: Europe's Copernicus Sentinel satellites track wildfires, floods, crops, sea level and ice for free. Portuguese firefighters and farmers use the data.

cards.title: Space debris
cards.text: Over a million pieces of debris larger than 1 cm orbit Earth at bullet-like speeds. A collision can create thousands more fragments.

cards.title: Satellite internet
cards.text: Constellations of thousands of satellites in low orbit provide fast internet anywhere, including ships, planes and remote villages. Astronomers worry about streaks in their images.

cards.title: Portugal in space
cards.text: Portugal joined ESA in 2000, founded the Portugal Space agency in 2019 and launched its first satellite, the PoSAT-1 microsatellite, back in 1993.

quiz.q: How many satellites does GPS need for a position?
quiz.explain: The fourth fixes the clock error.

quiz.q: Europe's satellite navigation system is called…

lessons.title: Astronomy's great pioneers
lessons.summary: How we learnt our place in the cosmos.

cards.title: Ancient astronomers
cards.text: Babylonians recorded eclipses for centuries; Greeks measured the Earth. Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes estimated Earth's circumference using shadows in two cities.

cards.title: Ptolemy's model
cards.text: Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, with planets moving on circles upon circles, predicted positions well enough to be used for 1,400 years.

cards.title: Copernicus
cards.text: In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus published his Sun-centred model, moving Earth from the centre of the universe. It took a century to be widely accepted.

cards.title: Tycho and Kepler
cards.text: Tycho Brahe made the most precise naked-eye measurements ever. His assistant Johannes Kepler used them to discover that planets move in ellipses.

cards.title: Galileo's trial
cards.text: Galileo's support for a Sun-centred system led to his trial by the Inquisition in 1633. He spent his last years under house arrest.

cards.title: Newton

steps: One law for apples and planets

cards.text: In 1687 Newton's *Principia* explained Kepler's laws with universal gravitation and laws of motion: the same physics on Earth and in the heavens.

cards.title: Herschel
cards.text: William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781, the first planet found with a telescope. His sister Caroline Herschel discovered several comets.

cards.title: Henrietta Leavitt

steps: Compare with how bright it looks

cards.text: In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt found that certain pulsing stars' periods reveal their true brightness, giving astronomers a cosmic measuring tape.

cards.title: Hubble and the galaxies
cards.text: In 1924 Edwin Hubble used Leavitt's method to show that Andromeda lies far outside the Milky Way. The universe suddenly contained countless galaxies.

cards.title: Pedro Nunes
cards.text: Portuguese mathematician Pedro Nunes (1502–1578) improved navigation, studying rhumb lines and inventing the nonius, a scale for precise angle readings. A lunar crater bears his name.

quiz.q: Who first measured Earth's circumference?
What did Kepler discover about orbits?

lessons.title: The future of space
lessons.summary: Where we're heading next.

cards.title: Back to the Moon

steps: Artemis II: crew around the Moon

cards.text: NASA's Artemis programme aims to return humans to the Moon for the first time since 1972 and build a long-term presence near the south pole.

cards.title: Why the lunar south pole?
cards.text: Permanently shadowed craters there hold water ice, which could provide drinking water, oxygen and rocket fuel.

cards.title: Gateway
cards.text: The Lunar Gateway is a planned small station orbiting the Moon, built by NASA, ESA, Japan and Canada, to support landings.

cards.title: Humans to Mars
cards.text: Sending people to Mars needs huge rockets, radiation protection, life support for years and a way home. Most plans aim for the 2030s or later.

cards.title: Space tourism
cards.text: Since 2021, private companies have flown paying tourists to the edge of space and to orbit. Tickets cost from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars.

cards.title: Mining asteroids
cards.text: Some asteroids contain metals like nickel, iron and platinum. Mining them could supply future space industry, but it isn't economic yet.

cards.title: Interstellar travel
cards.text: The nearest star is 4.2 light-years away; Voyager would take about 75,000 years. Ideas like tiny probes pushed by lasers might cut that to decades.

cards.title: Space telescopes to come
cards.text: Next-generation telescopes aim to photograph Earth-like exoplanets and analyse their air for signs of life, such as oxygen and methane together.

cards.title: Space law
cards.text: The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says no nation can claim the Moon or planets, and space is free for all to explore peacefully. Resource mining is still debated.

cards.title: Why explore?
cards.text: Space research gave us satellite navigation, weather forecasts, better medical imaging and water filters, and it answers the oldest question: are we alone?

quiz.q: Why is the Moon's south pole attractive?
quiz.explain: Water for air, drinking and fuel.

quiz.q: Which treaty forbids nations claiming the Moon?
